title: What time will the next ticket show?

beats.say: The last train to Harbor Point leaves at seventeen thirty. Keep the first copy. At the terminal, restore the twelve-hour template in Git. Look at the little window on the printer. What time will the next ticket show?
Send the same departure through again. Seventeen thirty. Follow the time across the perforation. Release two served this ticket. Its image still contains the compiled twenty-four-hour template.

Open the archive at release one. Load its saved image with the twelve-hour template. Print that departure once more. Five thirty P M. Both tickets name the same model. The stubs identify the releases that actually printed them. We will use that same observation to test a deployment assistant, decide who gets its replies, and bring a conversation home after an abort.

title: Hash retained bytes and the canonical manifest

beats.say: A release bundle records the components that produce behavior. Here the model pin stays fixed, while prompt and runtime bytes differ. We hash those retained bytes and place their pins in a canonical manifest. Hashing that manifest gives the complete bundle its release identity. The other policy and evaluation pins stay attached to it.

Keep the candidate's original prompt beside its bundle. Change just the sentence about checking claims. Read down the new column. Its prompt digest and release digest both change. The image digest stays put. Keeping the original bytes lets us run either version again.
A hosted model also needs the provider's strongest version contract and its effective settings. We will keep the original candidate for the rollout.

title: What did the worker load?

beats.say: Now take a deployment assistant. It looks for an approval record before it answers. Keep the model pin, tokenizer and template. Keep the compiled prompt and the build that produced it. A tool schema tells the assistant how to ask for evidence.

The policy, corpus and index determine what it may use. Pin the retrieval settings, serving image and decoding configuration too. Now change the output schema. An answer can be correct and still fail when the router expects version two and the worker returns version three.

The article records thirteen fields for this application. Your manifest needs the dependencies your workers actually use. Changing the compiled prompt and the image together tests that pair. It leaves their individual effects unresolved.

Here’s the file the worker loads. Its name matches the manifest. Overwrite that file in place. The name still matches, but look at the two digests now. At startup, compare the loaded bytes with the retained pin. Reject that worker when they differ.

Restore the pinned bytes, or register the changed bytes in a new bundle and evaluate it. Once a worker has loaded the intended bundle, record its resolved release on each request. Data permissions and evidence that an evaluation actually ran need their own checks.

To give two systems the same release ID, they must hash exactly the same bytes. The lab sorts JSON keys, removes optional whitespace, and hashes the UTF eight encoding. Store the evaluation report separately. It can name the finished release and have its own digest.
Putting a report containing the release ID inside the manifest would make the hash depend on itself. The screen shows a short prefix. The registry keeps the full digest.

title: Retain a usable version as well as its name

beats.say: On Monday the provider sends your requests to version A. On Tuesday it moves the same alias to version B. Your application stayed on the same release. To track which model you used, pin the most specific version the provider documents and record your request settings. Check how long that version will be available.

Send one saved input three times with the same effective settings. Two replies match and one differs. Even at temperature zero, providers can vary how they run a model. When a version or setting changes, register a new candidate and compare repeated regression cases.
Before a rollback, check that the stable endpoint still accepts requests. Here the provider has retired it.

The article’s registry checks the previous target before it moves a pointer. Follow production from stable to candidate and back. Someone who checks the target sees stable both times. Add a revision number and the two visits are easy to tell apart.
In production, authorize the writer, compare the target and revision in one atomic update, and keep a durable record of the change.

title: Artifacts stay fixed while pointers gain revisions

beats.say: Register the two bundles as immutable records. Each can now be fetched by its digest. Production points to stable. The canary pointer names candidate. Follow the production cable as the controller moves it. What fact would let a delayed writer detect a round trip?

Production moves to candidate, then returns to stable. The target looks familiar, but the revision has advanced. An old writer still expects the original revision. Its update is rejected. In a production registry, perform that comparison atomically, authenticate the writer, and retain the transition record.

title: Compute route quality and check the critical slice separately

beats.say: Count serving the answer as the positive decision. A true positive serves a supported request, a false positive serves an unsupported one, and a false negative abstains on a supported request.

Route F one is two times true positives divided by two times true positives plus false positives plus false negatives. It measures the routing decision. A separate claim-support review must check the generated answer.

Here are the counts on a separate worksheet. Ninety supported requests were served, five unsupported requests were served, and ten supported requests received an abstention. Double ninety to get one hundred eighty. Add five and ten below the line. One hundred eighty over one hundred ninety-five gives twelve thirteenths, about point nine two three.
That clears a point nine two average floor but the five unsupported serves still violate this exercise’s zero-count safety rule. A good average cannot cancel a critical failure.

The frozen reference gate also requires rollback-slice F one at least point nine, two hundred cases with complete support and latency coverage, report age from zero through twenty-four hours, and p ninety-five at most five hundred milliseconds. Missing, future-dated or timezone-free reports fail.
Include terminal errors and timeouts in the latency population. Pin the suite, evaluator and schema before comparing any threshold.

title: Replay the approval request

beats.say: Open request two oh five. The assistant said payment tests had approval to ship. The approval record was empty. Before testing the candidate, run the historical program. It serves the approval even with the support label set to false. That gives us a control.
Without it, a clean candidate result could just mean we changed the test.

Keep the question and its false support label fixed. Stable withholds the approval. Now try the candidate. It withholds too. The article checks that the model, corpus and evidence gate match. It runs a Boolean policy branch. The tool names, temperature and seed are recorded metadata.
Testing generated answers would also require the request and evidence bytes, the actual program and recorded tool results.

Here’s how to use a recorded tool result in a real replay. The trace contains a read of policy version seven. When the candidate asks for seven, give it the saved result. That keeps the evidence fixed and avoids repeating a production action.
Now change just the requested version to eight. The only saved result is still for seven. Can the harness use it?

Stop the replay here. The tool name matches. Its argument doesn’t. Report the differing call and get an approved source for version eight before making that comparison. With variable model outputs, repeat the matched runs and compare failure rates. Add this incident to the regression suite.
Passing it tells us what happened on this particular case.

title: Evaluation evidence must name this exact bundle

beats.say: The offline report is a receipt for one candidate, suite, schema and evaluator. Match those four entries. Two hundred cases have both checks. The report is two hours old. Route F one is point nine three. Rollback F one is point nine one. No unsupported approval was served. P ninety-five is four hundred seventy-two milliseconds. This report clears the offline gate.
Change only the evaluator on the receipt to version three. Could those same scores still qualify the release under the frozen policy?

Reject the report. The policy requires version two. Keep the reviewed case labels, authenticated results, component bytes and execution environment so an engineer can trace each total back to the run.

title: Which case is missing?

beats.say: The summary claims two hundred completed rows. Compare the first five result slips with the case numbers on the rack. Which expected case has no result?

Case three is missing. Case two was counted twice. Match the results to the expected case IDs and keep failures and timeouts in the count. Before the gate reads the totals, verify the report digest, who scored each case, what counted as support, and which runtime ran it.

Separate contract errors from numerical errors. A different evaluator, suite, schema or release makes otherwise strong numbers inapplicable. A missing metric is unknown. Reject booleans, numeric strings, negative values, not-a-number and infinity where finite measurements are required. If conversion to a float would overflow, reject the metric and keep the controller running.

Registration permits addressing a bundle. Passing this offline gate permits the next experiment. Moving a canary alias alone sends no requests. The router and exposure controller must actually admit traffic. These are different events, so record them separately instead of treating a green build or a newly registered artifact as production evidence.

title: Who gets the third reply?

beats.say: A policy question comes in. Stable sends its reply to the user. We also give the candidate a minimized copy. Its answer goes to an evaluator. That second path is a shadow.

To look up the policy, the worker needs the tool on its allowlist and a credential with permission to read it. Both checks pass for this lookup. Now try the deployment tool. The allowlist excludes it, and the credential only permits reads.
A hidden answer can still cause a real action if a worker has both permissions. Here the read-only credential and the tool allowlist prevent that deployment.

Now three users ask for policy checks. Stable returns three replies. On the shadow path, both waiting slots start empty. Put the first copy in one slot. Put the second in the other. A third copy arrives. Both slots are occupied. Who still gets a reply, and which comparison will be missing?

Drop the third copy. The third user still got a reply from stable. We admitted two copies for evaluation. We have no candidate result for the one we dropped. Count that gap, keep the workers and their costs separate, and check completed answers against their evidence.

title: Does agreeing make the answer right?

beats.say: In the article’s example, the worker replaces the ship number with a placeholder. Stable withheld approval. The simulated candidate withholds it too. Their routes agree, and the record supports withholding. The article computes those decisions from a supplied support label. It doesn’t generate either answer.
Replacing this one pattern removes the ship number. Other identifiers and secrets would need their own handling.

Sanitize the inputs before the queue, logs, or candidate can see them. If sanitizing changes retrieval, use equivalent inputs for both releases or measure that difference. Now suppose both releases serve the approval on that same empty record. They still agree. Both are wrong. Track support and answer quality alongside latency, drops and timeouts.

Look down the tool checks. The read on the first row has both permissions. On the second row, somebody supplied a write credential, but the deployment tool is off the list. On the last row, somebody allowed the tool, but the credential can only read.

Only the policy lookup can run. A flag saying side effects are disabled changes neither permission. Keep shadow workers bounded. Persist their work and results so a restart, a full queue, or a timeout shows up as missing coverage while stable keeps serving.

title: Where does turn four go?

beats.say: At ten percent, a canary sends some new conversations to the candidate. The router hashes each conversation ID to a bucket. Thread six lands in bucket six, below ten, so it goes to the candidate. Thread zero lands in bucket nineteen and goes to stable. The router saves each release on the first turn.
Widen the threshold to every new conversation. Thread zero now sends turn four. Its bucket is inside the widened band. Where does this request go?

Follow the route saved on turn one. Stable handles turn four. The router used the stored release before consulting the threshold. Now start a new conversation. It takes the candidate route because the wider threshold applies to first assignments.

title: New-conversation share and request exposure have different denominators

beats.say: Deterministic S H A two fifty-six buckets select new conversations; a shared durable store must atomically preserve their first resolved release with a defined expiry. Python’s process-dependent hash is unsuitable for cross-worker assignment. A later alias move or wider threshold does not silently rewrite an active conversation’s saved release under this normal-widening policy.

Count the ten newly assigned conversations. One got the candidate, so the conversation share is ten percent. Now count their requests. The candidate thread sent twenty and the other nine sent one each. Twenty out of twenty-nine requests reached the candidate, about sixty-nine percent. The same traffic gives two different fractions because we counted different things.

An abort overrides assignments to a failed release. Propagate that decision through routers and caches and verify resolved identities. If older code cannot read the conversation or tool state, pause, migrate or reset under a reviewed compatibility policy. Check the saved state before resuming the conversation.

title: Which rollout does this window describe?

beats.say: A request belongs to a release and to a particular rollout attempt. Check both IDs and the time interval. This policy accepts a window that ended within the last five minutes. It needs a thousand requests, with support, latency and transport checked for every one.

A candidate that withholds every answer could have a clean safety record. Did it help the people it could answer? We need at least a hundred answerable requests, including fifty rollback questions. In each group at least ninety percent must actually receive a useful answer.
Empty replies, errors and unnecessary abstentions count against it.

Choose the limits before looking at traffic. Our reference policy caps live p ninety-five at five hundred fifty milliseconds. Transport errors may affect at most one percent of requests. The separate shadow queue may drop at most two percent of comparisons.

The article’s shorter worksheet uses a five hundred millisecond ceiling. A latency of five hundred twenty would clear one ceiling and break the other. Keep each verdict with the policy that produced it.

These columns are two alternative samples. Start at one percent. Twelve hundred reviews found zero unsupported serves. Two transport errors in twelve hundred are about point one six seven percent. Divide useful answers by answerable requests in each group.

The results are ninety-four percent overall and ninety-two percent on rollback questions. This window clears the gates. Now look at the ten percent sample. Its usefulness is just as high overall, and its latency and transport pass too. Which row could still stop the canary?
A hundred twelve of eight thousand requests served an unsupported claim. That’s one point four percent. Abort this canary. The rule permits zero unsupported serves.

title: May this canary take more traffic?

beats.say: These six hundred requests came from this candidate on rollout fifty-two. Five hundred ninety-nine have a support review. Request ninety-eight is still waiting. Look at the two strips. Even if the missing review comes back clean, six hundred requests still falls short of a thousand.
Hold this canary at its present exposure while the evidence comes in.
Set that sample aside. In this independent window, all twelve hundred requests have a review. There are no unsupported serves. Check the experience limits beside the counts.

Responses meet the latency limit, two transport errors fit the error budget, and the separate shadow queue stayed under its drop limit. Now look at the answerable requests. Seven hundred fifty-two of eight hundred got a useful answer. Among the hundred rollback questions, ninety-two did.
Both groups clear ninety percent and have enough cases. Pass this window. The controller can take the next planned step.

Go back to the six hundred. The final review for request ninety-eight has arrived. The candidate served an approval with no record to support it. The reviewer matched that request to this release and this rollout. We’re still four hundred requests short of the minimum.
Should the canary keep serving until we reach a thousand, or should we stop its traffic now?

Stop candidate traffic now. One confirmed unsupported approval breaks the rule. The volume minimum tells us when we may widen. We already have the evidence we need to abort. Even the separate window that passed left us with a question about rare failures.

title: Zero observed failures still has a sample-size limit

beats.say: HOLD means stop widening while trustworthy evidence is missing. An under-sampled window or zero failures with incomplete reviews cannot pass. A correctly attributed confirmed unsupported serve can already trigger an abort, even below minimum volume or with missing latency.
Malformed support counters or wrong release attribution instead require investigation. Put an escalation timeout on missing telemetry so the experiment cannot linger unseen.

Compute what a zero count can establish under a separate statistical contract. For n independent trials with a fixed failure probability, correct classification and a sample size fixed in advance, the probability of zero failures is the quantity one minus the failure probability, raised to n.

Find the failure probability at which zero observed failures has probability alpha. Solve for the upper bound. It is one minus alpha raised to the power of one over n. For a one-sided ninety-five percent confidence bound, alpha is point zero five.

For twelve hundred zero-failure trials the upper bound is about point zero zero two four nine, or point two four nine percent. At that upper bound, about one request in four hundred would fail. Correlated conversations, missed failures or a decision to stop after seeing the results require a different analysis.

title: Abort a canary before promotion; roll back after it

beats.say: In the first drill, candidate has only the canary pointer. Abort removes its exposure, marks its assignments failed, and repoints canary to stable. Production has stayed on stable throughout.

Start a separate drill with production on stable. Promote the candidate to production. A later failure now affects that production target. Return production to stable and record a rollback. Keep both transitions. Previously delivered answers and external actions remain in the history. Verify subsequent requests on the restored release and check compatibility before resuming in-flight work.

title: Can stable take the load back?

beats.say: Production points to stable. The returning requests need a hundred replies a second. Read across the bar. Healthy, compatible workers can handle ninety. That leaves ten requests a second without capacity.
A self-hosted worker may still be loading weights, compiling, or reserving cache space while it waits for a GPU. With a hosted model, check the endpoint and its quota as well as your own workers.

Look at the next readiness receipt for the same stable release. Twenty more requests a second of capacity are ready. The demand mark stayed at a hundred. These workers can now carry the returning load with ten requests a second to spare. Rehearse the return under load and check the stable digest on actual requests.
That check tells you whether the pointer change reached the workers.

title: Which release answered request 272?

beats.say: Open request two seventy-two in the complete window on rollout fifty-two. Its serving trace names the candidate digest. Look up that digest in the release registry. The manifest names the suite and evaluator. Follow the retained report digest to the evidence used for the canary decision.

The transition records the actor and time, the expected stable target at revision one, and the new candidate target at revision two. Protect the audit store and retain the bytes those records refer to.

The article supplies a hypothetical history in which one window passes and another aborts. A running controller should record each transition as it happens. Workers record which bundle actually served. Suppose the trace loses its release ID. Can today’s alias fill that gap?

The observed release is unknown. Today's alias cannot fill that gap. A router may have cached an earlier target. Sampling, dropped spans and editable metadata can all break the chain. A protected audit store and collection coverage checks help you find those gaps.

Use the symptom to decide what to inspect next. An answer the router can’t parse points to the schema or serving image. If the answer parses but claims an approval the record doesn’t support, replay it with the pinned evidence.
If a supported answer is slow, check runtime capacity and decoding. If measurements are missing, hold exposure and repair collection. Save that reasoning alongside the alias change.

title: Assign each control to the system that can actually enforce it

beats.say: An artifact store or O C I registry retains verified component bytes. An owned release registry resolves complete manifests and enforces authorized atomic pointer revisions. M L flow aliases identify particular model versions; they need a surrounding manifest for prompt, corpus, policy and runtime.

MLflow deprecated its older fixed model stages. A model tagged for production identifies one component. Ask where you would look up the exact retrieval index and the compiled prompt that accompanied that model.

C I and a reviewed evaluator retain case outcomes and scorer provenance. Argo Rollouts can advance, pause or abort from configured analysis, with failed background analysis returning canary weight to zero in the documented example.

Basic canary weights may approximate traffic through replica counts; a compatible traffic router provides finer control. Your application separately owns persistent conversation assignments and the task’s support evaluator.

Application workers and the managed or self-hosted backend own ready capacity, dependency compatibility and availability. Collectors and protected evidence stores retain observed identities and outcomes. Feature flags can select a registered release, but record the resolved target at serving time. The trace then tells you which release answered even after the flag moves.

title: Can thread six come back?

beats.say: Your turn to run the canary. This is rollout seventy-three. Production points to stable. Only the canary points to the candidate. The window is fresh. Nine hundred of twelve hundred candidate requests have a support review. None has confirmed an unsupported approval. Latency and transport look healthy.
Do you widen, hold this exposure, or stop the canary?

Hold the exposure. We’ve reviewed seventy-five percent. Three hundred outcomes are still unknown. Here comes a review from rollout seventy-two. That approval was unsupported, but it belongs with the earlier attempt. The count here stays at nine hundred.

Now a separate review arrives for request nine oh one on seventy-three. It confirms an unsupported approval. That brings the count to one in nine hundred and one reviews. Stop candidate traffic. Block the saved assignments to this release and move the canary pointer back to stable. Record a canary abort. Production stayed where it was.

Now both pointers select stable. This time the returning traffic needs a hundred fifty requests a second. The first set of healthy workers can take a hundred thirty-four. How much capacity are we missing?

Sixteen requests a second have nowhere to go. A later receipt shows ready capacity of one hundred sixty. Bring thread six to the stable worker. Its saved conversation uses version two. The shipment sits under ship I D. The stable worker reads version one, with the value under ship.
The worker has room for this request. Look at the two field names. Can this conversation resume with its shipment intact?

Pause thread six. Stable cannot read this state. If there is no compatible migration, keep the conversation paused or use a reviewed reset. Here a reviewed migration copies the shipment into the ship field and writes version one. Read it back before admitting the request.

Resume one request under the returning load. The worker records stable's digest, thread six, and shipment forty-four twelve. Follow that value back to the saved conversation. We have seen the same shipment read successfully on the release that actually served the request.
